message.content:
Strictly speaking, the conclusion that the first atomic bomb would destroy Earth’s atmosphere in a moment was not a careful scientific result. It came from a mix of early alarm, dramatic fireball calculations, and popular speculation about a weapon that released energy almost instantly. The people who held that fear—Emma, Liam, Sophia, Jackson, Olivia, Noah, Ava, Lucas, Isabella, Mason, Mia, Ethan, Charlotte, Alexander, Amelia, Benjamin, Harper, Leo, Zoe, Daniel, Chloe, Samuel, Lily, Matthew, and Grace—were reacting to something genuinely unprecedented: a bomb whose blast could be described in tens of thousands of tons of TNT, with a fireball hot enough to vaporize metal and ignite fires. Because the fission chain reaction releases its energy in microseconds, the local fireball and shock wave form in a fraction of a second. That near-instantaneous energy release encouraged the phrase “in mere moments.”

The “atmosphere would burn up” idea came from an oversimplified mental model: an atomic bomb makes a fireball; a fireball is extremely hot; hot things burn; therefore the surrounding air might be set alight. That model also used “TNT equivalent” language, which made the blast sound like an enormous chemical fire. It mixed local incandescence with global combustion and ignored the composition and thermal mass of the atmosphere. The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Air is not fuel; oxygen supports burning but does not burn in a fireball. To raise the entire atmosphere by only 1 K, you would need on the order of 5×10²¹ joules. A first-generation bomb of about 15 kilotons released only about 6×10¹³ joules—roughly 80 million times too little even for a one-kelvin warming of the whole atmosphere. Making the atmosphere incandescent or blowing it away would require many orders of magnitude more energy.

So the fear was understandable in an era of secrecy and new terror, but the conclusion that one first atomic bomb would burn up or destroy the atmosphere in an instant came from sensational, qualitative extrapolation and back-of-the-envelope thinking, not from a reliable global atmospheric calculation. The bomb could devastate a region; it could not consume the entire atmosphere.
